t: Damage comes in three brackets that multiply: items add to a flat bracket, shrine stat offers add to a % bracket, and the Damage Tome is its own multiplier. ( Core math ) Crit chance past 100% overcrits, and the multiplier grows quadratically: 1 crit ×2, 2 ×4, 3 ×6.25, 4 ×9. Most proc items have diminishing returns built in. Dragonfire, Ice Cube, Lightning Orb, Power Gloves and Key use x / (x + k), so the 10th copy adds far less than the first. Enemy HP in the final swarm multiplies by 4 every minute, and their damage doubles every minute. Damage alone stops keeping up around 12:00; long runs

Megabonk is a 3D roguelike survival game in the "bullet heaven" style. You pick a character and run around a generated map while your weapons attack on their own. Enemies pour in, killing them gives XP and gold, and every level-up lets you pick an upgrade. A run lasts until you die or beat the final boss, and your score is mostly how many enemies you killed. This page is the big picture. The other

Survive each stage's timer while getting stronger. Each stage is a fixed-length script of waves, swarms and minibosses (10:00, 9:00 and 8:00 on Forest and Desert; one 16:00 stage on Graveyard). Kill the stage boss. Killing it, or letting the timer run out, starts the final swarm : an endless flood of ghosts that gets tougher every minute. Take the portal to the next stage. Your tier decides how many stages you play: Tier 1 is one stage, Tier 2 two, Tier 3 three. Beat the final boss. After the tier's last stage comes the final-boss map: Ent on Forest, Pharaoh on Desert, Ghost King on Graveyard.

Four kinds of power stack together: Weapons attack automatically and level up through offers. You start with 2 slots and can buy up to 4 with Silver; bought slots stay until you refund them. See Weapons . Tomes (2 slots, up to 4 the same way) each raise one stat per level: damage, attack speed, size, Luck, XP and so on. See Tomes . Items come from chests, shrines and vendors, and there's no slot limit. Most stack: 10 copies do 10 times as much, or less where the code adds diminishing returns. A few are capped: Anvil 1, Overpowered Lamp 2, Joe's Dagger 10, Za Warudo 25 per run. See Items . Stat

It's fully 3D. You move, jump and fall across hilly terrain, and your stats include jump height, extra jumps, slam and fall-damage reduction. Terrain matters for dodging and for reaching shrines and chests. Most items stack without limit. Most survivor games cap items; here 30 copies of one item is normal in a long run (only Anvil, Overpowered Lamp, Joe's Dagger and Za Warudo have caps), and crit chance past 100% "overcrits" for ×4, ×6.25 and more. Each character starts with one weapon and has a passive that grows with level. Dicehead, for example, gets a free random stat (Gamba) every level-up. Characters also have different base stats. See Characters .

Every run builds a new map from a random seed. The terrain and the placement of everything on it change each time, but the amounts are fixed by the code ( SpawnInteractables , RandomObjectPlacer ): Each shrine slot becomes a random type: Shady Guy, Moai, Boss Curse, Magnet or Challenge, plus Bald Heads on Graveyard. So two maps always have the same number of chests and shrine slots, but one might have six Shady Guys and no Moai while the next has the reverse. Some things are rolled when the map loads and never change: each Shady Guy's and Microwave's rarity, for example. That's why seed scanni

Enemies scale on three clocks: The whole run: +10% HP and +2.8% damage per minute. This never resets. The stage: stage 2 enemies start at about 30× base HP, stage 3 at about 150×. The final swarm: HP ×4 and damage ×2 every minute. This resets each stage. Difficulty and your tier multiply all of it. That's why a build that was overkill on stage 1 can stall on stage 3, and why the final swarm always ends a run sooner or later.

Silver earned in runs and quests (achievements) unlocks new characters, weapons, items and tomes, and buys permanent upgrades such as extra weapon and tome slots. You can also toggle items out of the pool, so chests only roll what you want. Every unlock is listed on Quests & unlocks and Challenges .

Every stat is held as three parts and combined the same way ( StatComponents.GetFinalValue ): Final = (base + flat bonuses) × (1 + sum of % bonuses) × (product of × multipliers) Which bonus goes in which part is set by its modify type in the code: So for Damage, the base is 1.0 and items stack inside the flat part: 5 Gym Sauces make it 1.5. Shrine Damage offers then add to the % bracket, and the Damage Tome multiplies everything. Spreading Damage across all three brackets beats piling it into one.

t: Armor and Evasion don't add up in a straight line. Each point is worth a bit less than the one before, so you can never reach 100%. The stat screen shows them as percentages, but the game stores them as plain numbers: 50% Armor on the stat screen is 0.5 in the formulas below , and 100% is 1.0. Hit = weapon damage × Damage stat (all three brackets) × crit multiplier × Crit damage Weapon damage is the weapon's own Damage stat (base plus its upgrade lines). Aegis adds your Thorns to it. Crit chance = your Crit chance + the weapon's Crit chance. On-hit items can add per-attack modifiers just before the hit (Boss Buster +15% to elites and bosses, Tactical Glasses +20% above 90% HP, Eagle Claw to airborne enemies, Giant Fork's Megacrit, Phantom Shroud). Execute (Dexecutioner, Ninja, Joe's Dagger): normal enemies that can be executed die outright; bosses, and enemies flagged as not executa

The game rolls how many crits a hit gets: one guaranteed crit for each full 100% of crit chance, plus one more with the leftover chance. 230% = 2 crits, with a 30% chance of 3. The formula is (1 + crits ÷ 2)², except that one crit is ×2. That multiplier is then multiplied by Crit damage (base ×1.0). Example: you have 230% crit chance. The full 200% gives 2 guaranteed crits. The leftover 30% is the chance of a third. 70% of hits get 2 crits: (1 + 2 ÷ 2)² = 2² = ×4 . 30% of hits get 3 crits: (1 + 3 ÷ 2)² = 2.5² = ×6.25 . On average: 0.7 × 4 + 0.3 × 6.25 = ×4.68 , before Crit damage.

Every on-hit roll is chance × the weapon's proc coefficient ( ItemUtility.TryProc ). Where an item's chance can pass 100% (Moldy Cheese, Snek's burst, Unstable Transfusion, Bloody Cleaver, Golden Glove), each full 100% is a guaranteed proc and only the leftover is rolled. Example: you hold 5 Dragonfire (60%, from the table below) and hit with the Axe, whose proc coefficient is 0.7. Each Axe hit has 60% × 0.7 = 42% to proc. The same 5 Dragonfire on a Sniper Rifle (1.5) would be 60% × 1.5 = 90%. Each weapon's proc coefficient is on the Weapons page. Items whose chance slows down with more copies

Damage taken = enemy damage × (1 − armor reduction) × (1 − damage reduction) , minimum 1. Example: a ghost hits for 1,000. You have 150% Armor (67% blocked) and no other damage reduction. You take 1,000 × (1 − 0.67) = 330 . Against boss attacks your armor counts half ; against the final boss it counts 75% . Some attacks ignore armor. Evasion is a chance to dodge a hit entirely. Shield is a separate pool, taken from the Shield stat as a whole number. Overheal cap = Max HP × Overheal. Lifesteal works like crits: one guaranteed heal per full 100%, plus a chance for one more.

Many items and effects don't use your weapon's damage. They use a player number called base damage: 8 + your character level , recalculated every level-up. Burn, Cursed Doll (against bosses), Holy Book, Energy Core, Soul Harvester, the elemental gloves and Bloodmark all scale with it, together with your Damage stat.

XP needed to go from level L to L + 1 ( XpUtility ): 5 + 5.325 × L^1.065 (level 1 → 2 is 7). The level cap is 9,999 . In words: each level costs a little more than the one before, growing slightly faster than straight-line. Going from level 1,000 to 2,000 takes about 3× the XP it took to reach 1,000 in the first place. Example: a run at level 2,000 has collected about 16.9 million XP. Reaching 4,000 needs about 70 million in total, roughly 4× as much again. XP per kill: each enemy has its own XP value in the enemy data, multiplied by your XP gain. Elites give 10× XP. All debuffs tick 2 times per second ( DebuffUtility.debuffTicksPerSecond = 2 ). Their length in ticks is round(2 × duration × Duration multiplier). Re-applying a debuff lengthens it only if the new duration is longer than what's left; the two never add up.

Damage per tick = stacks × Damage × Poison damage , never less than 1 per stack. Two ticks a second. Example: an enemy has 10 poison stacks, your Damage stat is ×2.0 and your Poison damage is ×1.0. Each tick deals 10 × 2.0 × 1.0 = 20 , twice a second, so 40 damage per second for as long as the stacks last. No stack cap. Every application adds stacks. Not affected by crits, weapon damage or boss damage. Reduced by enemy armor; boosted by Elite damage against elites. Can't trigger on-hit items (proc coefficient 0). Moldy Cheese past 100%. Each stage runs a fixed script from the map data. Times count up from the start of the stage. A new enemy type joins the pool every 60 seconds. Which miniboss you get: every miniboss event draws from the map's miniboss list without repeats until the list is used up, then starts over ( SummonerController.EventMiniboss ). Using a Boss Curse shrine adds 1 to a counter on the stage's game manager ( GameManager.bossCurses ). Nothing in the code carries it over, and recorded runs matched a per-stage count (2 curses → 3 Chunkhams on stage 1; 5 curses → 6 Stone Golems on stage 2). Every miniboss event spawns 1 + curses minibosses , and the stage boss spawns as 1 + curses bosses . Every boss has its HP multiplied by 1 + 0.16 × curses. Boss HP also gets a stage multiplier: ×2.5 on stage 2 and ×5 on stage 3. Bosses can't be killed by Bob's Light or executes; Cursed Doll only does 0.7 × (8 + level) to them.

Every rarity roll that uses Luck goes through the same function ( Rarity.CalculateRarityWeights ): weight of a rarity × 1.5^(−steps below the top rarity × 1.5 × ln(1 + Luck)) , then normalised. In plain terms each step down in rarity is scaled by (1 + Luck)^−0.61. That's about ×1.5 at Luck 100%, ×1.9 at 200% and ×2.3 at 300%. Luck keeps helping but with diminishing returns. h: What the code changes about common advice
t: Cursed Doll is the late-swarm engine. It ignores enemy HP entirely (30% of max HP per second on non-bosses), so it keeps killing when the final swarm's HP bonus reaches thousands. Against bosses it's weak. Bob's Light is the other one. It instantly kills every non-boss in its radius; stack copies to reach the 5 s cooldown (14 copies) and 250 radius (20 copies). Proc items fall off. Dragonfire, Ice Cube, Lightning Orb and Power Gloves give much less per copy after the first few. Lightning Orb caps at 90%. Moldy Cheese and Snek don't fall off. Every weapon's numbers from the game's weapon data, how fast each one attacks, and how each tome changes it. Unlock requirements are on Quests & unlocks .

Upgrades: each weapon upgrade raises a few of that weapon's stat lines by the Common amount × the offer's rarity (×1.0 Common up to ×2.0 Legendary). Anvil adds one more line to future offers. Level cap: 40, plus 10 for the first Pot (Stainless Steel) and 1 less for each extra copy (never below +2). Slots: 2 to start, up to 4 with the Weapon Slots upgrade. See the FAQ for 2 vs 3 vs 4. Your stats apply on top: the weapon's damage × your Damage stat, its crit chance + yours, and so on. The tome section below has every formula.

One attack cycle = cooldown ÷ Attack Speed + projectiles × shot interval , where the shot interval = max(burst time ÷ projectiles, minimum interval) ÷ Attack Speed. So more projectiles usually cost no extra time: the burst is spread over the same burst time, until the shots hit the weapon's minimum interval. Attack Speed (Cooldown Tome) shortens everything.

Attacks/s is projectiles fired per second at base (Attack Speed 100%, no Quantity). Proc rolls/s is attacks/s × proc coefficient: how often the weapon rolls on-hit items like Big Bonk, Lightning Orb and Dragonfire against one enemy. Weapons that pierce, bounce or hit an area roll once per enemy hit, so in a crowd they roll many times more. Proc coefficients come straight from the weapon data ( procCoefficient ). Contact weapons (Aegis, Chunkers, Dragon's Breath, Space Noodle, Flamewalker) roll whenever they touch an enemy, so their rate depends on the crowd, not on a cycle.

Does Difficulty make enemies tougher, or just more of them? Both. Each 100% Difficulty adds: +110% enemy HP (1.1 × Difficulty) +100% enemy damage (1 × Difficulty) +0.7 to the spawn multiplier (0.7 × Difficulty), which sets how fast enemies spawn and how fast the final swarm refills: 1 + 0.7 × Difficulty + 0.4 × stage. Example: at 100% Difficulty on stage 1, the spawn multiplier is 1 + 0.7 = 1.7, so 70% more enemies than at 0%. They also have 110% more HP and hit twice as hard.

h: 4. The final swarm: where the kills are
t: The final swarm starts at the stage boss kill or the timer, whichever comes first, so killing the boss early starts the farm early . Inside it: Enemies refill toward 400 (first 2 minutes) then 300, at a rate that rises with Difficulty : the spawn multiplier is 1 + 0.7 × Difficulty + 0.4 × stage. More Difficulty = faster refill = more kills per minute. Enemy HP gains +3 at 1 minute, +15 at 2, +63 at 3, +1,023 at 5. A weak build's damage stops keeping up within a few minutes; a strong one (crit past 200%, Big Bonk, Lightning Orb) keeps the full kill rate up to the 12:00 Red Ghost switch, as the

The swarm swaps its ghost type on a fixed clock: Greater Ghost at 1:00, Purple Ghost at 6:00 (not executable, so Joe's Dagger and executes stop working), and Red Ghost at 12:00 . Counting the short delay after the boss dies, that's roughly 13 minutes after the boss kill. Red Ghosts are the wall: 100 base HP, speed 10 (×1.2 in the swarm = 12), knockback resistance 50, flying, not executable. Bob's Light only kills a Red Ghost 33% of the time ( KillEnemyTrigger.chanceToOneshotRedGhosts ). By 12 minutes enemy damage has gained +4,095: a Red Ghost (30 base damage) hits for about 135,000. No HP or shield pool keeps up, so long swarm runs survive by not getting hit . The code expects this: three rules in EnemyStats only switch on far into a swarm. Also, after any hit you get 0.15 seconds of invulnerability ( MyPlayer.OnDamage ). What that means for a build: Evasion is the defence that scales. It ignores how big the hit is. Real dodge chance is E / (E + 1) × 0.999: Evasion 1 = 50%, 4 = 80%, 10 = 91%, 20 = 95%, 50 = 98%. The 361k run had 0.62 (38%).

h: Is it better to run 2, 3 or 4 weapon slots?
t: You start with 2 weapon slots and 2 tome slots . Each kind gets up to 2 more from the Weapon Slots and Tome Slots shop upgrades (unlocked at 25 and 45 quests for weapons, 35 and 55 for tomes). t: What's the highest kill count possible? 16,777,216. The top three leaderboard runs all stop at exactly that number. The game keeps run stats, kills included, as 32-bit floats ( RunStats stores a Dictionary<string, float> ), and 16,777,216 = 2²⁴ is the largest whole number a float counts exactly. Past it, adding 1 kill doesn't change the number, so the counter stops there. Does a chest get more expensive if I wait? No. The price depends only on how many chests you've opened this run.
